In arXiv 2502.00012, the precautionary principle relates to AI governance by supporting preemptive regulatory intervention before harms have fully materialized or risks are conclusively established. This principle suggests that when there are threats of serious or irreversible damage, the lack of full scientific certainty should not be a reason to postpone cost-effective measures to prevent potential harm from AI technologies.

A complexity-related consideration that modifies the application of the precautionary principle is the recognition that many AI systems exhibit properties characteristic of complex systems, such as nonlinearity, emergence, feedback loops, and cascading effects. These characteristics imply that risks from AI may spread swiftly and exponentially, leading to grave systemic risks. Therefore, the costs of delaying regulatory intervention until more complete information is available can be significantly higher than the costs of early intervention. This understanding encourages regulators to act on the basis of incomplete information and to familiarize themselves with the patterns of complex systems to evaluate potential risks and design appropriate interventions.
